name: Phone at eye level / tech neck avoidance

lead: This habit means lifting your phone toward eye level so your head does not tilt down. People use it to avoid tech neck, also called text neck, and link it to a better neck line and jawline.

The chain is the phone held at eye level, less head-down neck flexion, then better neck posture. The reasoning is biomechanical: a head held forward and down loads the neck more than an upright head. A 2023 scoping review found that text neck lacks a consensus definition across the literature, and no study tests the habit or its appearance effect.

paras: People hold the phone higher, rest the elbows on the body or a desk, use a stand or phone holder, and take breaks from long head-down sessions. It is a behavior change that applies immediately to how the head is carried.
No notable risks are described. Holding a phone higher is a behavioral change only; arm fatigue is a practical downside.

angle.text: Holding the phone at eye level keeps the head up instead of down, which posture and looksmaxxing circles link to a better neck line and jawline. The path runs from the phone held high to less head-down flexion to better neck posture. Tech neck lacks an agreed definition, and the appearance link comes from anecdote.

lead: Lifting the phone toward eye level is a free, no-equipment posture habit that people use to keep the head stacked over the shoulders, which they say gives a cleaner profile, a more defined jaw-to-neck line and a taller, more upright presence.

Holding a phone at eye level to avoid tech neck, also called text neck, is a posture habit intended to keep the head over the shoulders instead of tilted down and forward while using a device. In looksmaxxing and posture communities it is linked to neck posture, the position of the chin and the visible lines of the jaw and neck [1].

The appearance chain people describe is positional: a head that sits forward of the shoulders places the ear ahead of the shoulder line and pushes the chin forward, a look Wikipedia compares to a dowager's hump, now seen in younger people; raising the screen is meant to reduce the time spent in that position [1]. A related belief connects repeated neck flexion to skin creasing and a softer jawline, sometimes labelled tech neck lines [2].

Researchers have not tested the habit itself. A 2023 scoping review found that text neck is widely called a global epidemic but lacks a consensus definition across the peer-reviewed literature [3]. Related work has examined questionnaires on symptoms and preventive measures such as breaks and ergonomic tools [4], skin treatments for neck lines [2] and posture-related bone changes [5].
infobox: Text neck, tech neck, forward head posture
Raised screens, laptop stands, regular breaks [4]

paras: A scoping review of peer-reviewed articles using the terms text neck or tech neck found inconsistent definitions, which the authors said challenges researchers and clinicians [3]. Wikipedia's article on forward head posture describes smartphone, tablet and laptop use as a commonly proposed contributor and notes that these devices cannot be set up as ergonomically as desktop screens [1]. Hunching is also linked to occupations including dentists, surgeons, hairdressers, nurses, chefs, teachers and computer workers [1]. Recent commentary calls tech neck a silent pandemic reshaping the spine [6].

Wikipedia describes the visual pattern of forward head posture as the ear sitting ahead of the shoulder, the chin jutting forward and the upper back curving forward [1]. Proponents of eye-level phone use describe this as the posture to avoid for a cleaner profile and for neck comfort.

A 2023 study of a skin treatment framed neck and jawline ageing as including wrinkling, laxity, loss of mandibular contour, submental fat accumulation and prominent platysma bands, and described early intervention for younger people with tech neck lines [2]. A 2026 orthodontic review discussed tech neck in relation to screen-time overload and dental and facial development [7].

Wikipedia's forward head posture article describes the extreme pattern: the earlobe ahead of a vertical line through the shoulder, the chin poking forward, and in severe cases the back of the skull in front of the breastbone [1]. It also describes 'swan-necking', in which the lower neck bends backward when looking up while the upper back stays hunched [1]. Posture-focused communities connect that pattern to a visible double chin, a shortened-looking neck and rounded shoulders, and treat a neutral head position as part of a taller, more open frame; these are descriptions of how people judge profile photos and video rather than results from controlled studies.

Wikipedia states that hunching raises the effective load on the neck several times over upright posture because of the longer moment arm, citing a 2014 estimate of roughly 10 pounds of added cervical load per inch of forward head position, with the page flagging parts of this material as weakly sourced [1]. It cites a 2019 meta-analysis that found a correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not adolescents, and a Finnish adolescent study linking over two hours a day of computer use to increased musculoskeletal pain [1].

A 2025 cross-sectional pilot questionnaire study explored neck pain, back pain and eye strain and how ergonomic tools, break frequency and posture awareness related to symptom intensity [4]. A 2024 study examined instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization for tech neck [8].

According to Wikipedia, thoracic joints can become stiff in a flexed position, surrounding connective tissue shortens, back support muscles weaken and stretch, and the deep neck flexors weaken so that the chin protrudes further [1]. Children may be at higher risk because their heads are large relative to their bodies [1]. The article links a reported rise in upper back and neck pain in the decade before 2016 to the spread of portable devices, and cites a figure of 4.43 billion mobile phone users worldwide in 2015 [1].

The same page gives point prevalence of adult neck pain across studies as ranging from 5.9 to 22.2 percent, and notes that the article itself carries warnings about weak sourcing, so figures should be read as indicative [1].

Common approaches described in posture communities and ergonomics literature include raising the device or screen toward eye level, using stands, taking breaks and strengthening exercises for the upper back and deep neck flexors; Wikipedia lists strengthening the mid and lower back and deep neck flexors, stretching the upper trapezius and thoracic mobilization among combined approaches for forward head posture [1].

The reference article suggests a combined approach: strengthening mid and lower back muscles, shoulder-blade retractors and the deep neck flexors, stretching the upper trapezius, manual work on tight tissue, and breaks plus a proper screen set-up during device use [1]. Other approaches it lists include physical therapy, yoga, Pilates and the Alexander Technique [1]. In posture communities the eye-level habit is the simplest piece of this: propping the phone on a stand or bringing the elbows up so the screen sits near eye height rather than lowering the head.

No studies found testing holding a phone at eye level as an intervention for appearance. Related research exists. A 2025 pilot questionnaire study explored symptoms, posture and preventive measures such as breaks and ergonomic tools [4]. A 2023 prospective open-label single-centre study examined a topical and device treatment for tech neck lines and wrinkles in Chinese women, addressing skin rather than posture [2]. A 2024 study examined instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization in tech neck [8]. A 2024 preprint compared bone changes at the skull base in modern and ancient populations in relation to tech neck posture [5]. Reviews in 2026 discussed tech neck as a spinal and orthodontic topic [7][6].

timeline.event: A widely cited estimate of added cervical load with forward head position is published [1].
Meta-analysis finds correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults [1].
Scoping review finds no consensus definition of text neck [3].
Pilot questionnaire study on tech neck symptoms and preventive measures [4].
